title: 5 Credentialing Costs That Don't Show Up in Your CVO Contract
summary: Your CVO contract is just one line item. Here are five credentialing costs most health plans aren't measuring, and the formulas to calculate each one.
body_markdown:
Most health plan finance leaders can pull their CVO contract number in minutes. What takes longer, and what most organizations can't answer with confidence, is what credentialing is actually costing them across the full operational model.


‍


Those are two different figures. And the gap between them is where the real exposure sits.


‍


I explored this recently for[Becker's Payer Issues](https://www.beckerspayer.com/payer/you-know-what-youre-spending-on-credentialing-you-dont-know-what-its-costing-you/) , laying out a framework for calculating the true cost of provider credentialing across five dimensions that rarely appear in any budget conversation. This post works through what that means in practice for health plan finance and operations leaders, and what a more complete cost picture changes about the decisions those leaders need to make.


‍


## **Why the CVO Contract Line Isn't the Whole Number**


‍


The CVO per-file fee is the most visible credentialing cost because it shows up in a contract. It's also the easiest figure to compare at renewal time, which makes it easy to treat as a proxy for total credentialing spend. Most organizations do.


‍


The problem is that the contract line doesn't capture what happens around the CVO. It doesn't reflect the revenue that doesn't arrive while providers wait for approval. It doesn't count the internal staff hours spent resolving incomplete files. It doesn't quantify the claims exposure that accumulates during monitoring gaps. And for Medicare Advantage plans, it has no line that connects directory accuracy to Star Rating bonus revenue.


‍


Five cost dimensions sit outside the contract, and all five are measurable with data most health plans already have.


‍


## **What Are the Five Overlooked Credentialing Cost Dimensions?**


‍


### **1. Network Access Delay Cost**


When a provider spends 60 to 120 days waiting for credentialing approval, they aren't seeing members. For high-demand specialties or underserved markets, that delay has a direct revenue consequence. The formula: average encounters per provider per month, multiplied by average days in the credentialing queue, multiplied by average per-encounter margin. The result reframes[provider onboarding speed](https://verifiable.com/provider-intake) as a revenue conversation, not just an operational metric.


‍


### **2. Cost Per Credentialing Event**


Total staff hours multiplied by burdened rate, divided by[credentialing events](https://verifiable.com/credentialing-software) processed monthly. This unit metric gives finance and operations a shared basis for credentialing investment decisions. Per-file fee structures create a direct relationship between network growth and vendor cost with no built-in volume efficiency. As networks expand into behavioral health, new geographies, or new lines of business, that cost compounds.


‍


### **3. Fraud and Claims Risk During Monitoring Gaps**


Providers who pass initial credentialing can still introduce financial and regulatory risk when monitoring functions as a one-time checkpoint rather than a continuous process. Claims paid to sanctioned providers during a monitoring gap represent measurable, recoverable losses. The exposure is a function of monitoring lag, the time between a provider status change and system detection, multiplied by claims volume passing through that window.[Regulatory scrutiny](https://verifiable.com/blog/the-credentialing-compliance-environment-changed-most-health-plans-are-still-catching-up) of monitoring gaps is intensifying.


‍


### **4. Incomplete Credentialing Event Cost**


When a CVO returns a file that doesn't meet full compliance requirements, someone on the health plan's team finishes it. That means internal staff dedicated not to processing new credentialing events, but to resolving incomplete ones: collecting missing documentation, clearing outstanding requirements, and advancing files to the point where they can move forward. The formula: files returned incomplete per month, multiplied by average internal hours to resolve, multiplied by burdened hourly rate. This cost sits entirely outside the CVO contract and often goes uncounted when organizations calculate total credentialing spend.


‍


### **5. Regulatory and Star Rating Revenue Exposure**


For Medicare Advantage plans, CAHPS access-to-care scores feed directly into Star Ratings, and Star Ratings feed directly into quality bonus payments. The program distributed more than $11.8 billion across MA plans in 2024, according to research published in JAMA Network Open. Directory accuracy, which flows directly from credentialing infrastructure, is a direct input into those scores. The calculation: member count, multiplied by current directory accuracy rate, multiplied by per-member revenue impact per rating point. For MA plans, this connects credentialing performance to the quality bonus revenue conversation directly.


‍


## **How Do You Calculate the True Cost of Credentialing?**


‍


Running all four formulas produces a credentialing cost baseline most organizations don't have. That baseline is what makes investment decisions defensible and ROI measurable over time.


‍


The data required isn't proprietary or difficult to source. Encounter volume, credentialing queue timelines, staff hours, burdened rates, and vendor per-file fees are figures most operations teams can pull. The issue isn't availability. It's that no one has built these formulas into how credentialing performance gets reported.


‍


Three questions tend to accelerate the internal conversation for finance leaders who want to start:


‍


1. What is the true cost per credentialing event, calculated per unit against actual volume rather than as a total budget line? This number should account for internal staffing and incomplete file resolution, not just the CVO fee.
2. What is the monitoring lag, and what financial liability does that gap represent? As regulatory attention on this figure grows, having a precise and defensible answer becomes increasingly important.
3. For Medicare Advantage business, what is the estimated Star Rating revenue exposure if directory accuracy is off by five percent? This is the calculation that connects credentialing infrastructure directly to quality bonus revenue.


‍


## **What Changes When Health Plans Do the Math**


‍


The organizations investing in credentialing infrastructure today aren't doing it because the technology is new. They're doing it because they've run the numbers, and the numbers changed what credentialing looks like in the budget conversation.


‍


Slow credentialing delays network access and the revenue that comes with it. Manual monitoring creates claims exposure that accumulates until it surfaces in an audit. Incomplete credentialing events generate staffing costs that compound in the background. Directory inaccuracy puts Star Rating revenue at risk in ways that are fully quantifiable at scale.


‍


None of these are theoretical. All of them are calculable with data most health plans already hold. Credentialing will keep getting treated as overhead until someone decides the numbers are worth knowing. For the finance and operations leaders who make that call, the numbers tend to do the rest.

The questions below address what health plan finance and operations leaders are most actively asking about credentialing cost, monitoring, and compliance exposure.


‍


## **Frequently Asked Questions**


‍


### **What is the true cost of provider credentialing for health plans?**


The true cost of provider credentialing includes at least five dimensions beyond the CVO contract: network access delay cost (revenue lost while providers wait for approval), cost per credentialing event (staff hours plus vendor fees calculated per unit), fraud and claims exposure during monitoring gaps, incomplete credentialing event cost (internal staff time spent resolving returned files), and directory accuracy risk to Star Rating bonus revenue. Most health plans track only the CVO per-file fee. The full cost, calculated across all five dimensions, is typically materially higher.


‍


### **How do you calculate cost per credentialing event?**


Cost per credentialing event is calculated as total internal staff hours multiplied by the burdened hourly rate, divided by the number of credentialing events processed per month, then added to the CVO per-file fee and any incomplete file resolution cost. This unit metric gives finance and operations a shared, defensible basis for credentialing investment decisions and for evaluating whether the current operational model delivers value relative to alternatives.


‍


### **What is credentialing monitoring lag and why does it matter?**


Monitoring lag is the time between a provider status change (such as a license sanction or exclusion) and the health plan's detection of that change. It matters because claims paid to sanctioned providers during that window represent measurable, recoverable losses. Regulators are paying increasing attention to this number. Health plans with continuous monitoring infrastructure reduce both the financial exposure and the audit risk associated with this gap.


‍


### **How does provider credentialing affect Medicare Advantage Star Ratings?**


Directory accuracy, which depends directly on credentialing infrastructure, is an input into CAHPS access-to-care scores, which feed into Medicare Advantage Star Ratings. Star Ratings determine eligibility for quality bonus payments, a program that distributed more than $11.8 billion across MA plans in 2024, according to JAMA Network Open. A five percent decline in directory accuracy can have a quantifiable impact on Star Rating scores and the bonus revenue tied to them.


‍


### **What credentialing costs are typically missing from health plan budgets?**


Three credentialing cost dimensions most commonly go unmeasured: incomplete credentialing event cost (internal staff hours spent resolving files that CVOs return incomplete), network access delay cost (revenue not generated while providers wait in the credentialing queue), and regulatory exposure tied to directory accuracy and Star Rating performance. All three are calculable with data most health plans already have. The gap isn't data availability. It's that these dimensions haven't been built into how credentialing performance gets reported to finance leadership.
